blockers.message: the review record has no `## code.review` section, while roles were active at it
R-security-1 (API tokens are stored in clear in the database) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it
R-security-2 (The Authorization header, and so every API token, is written to the logs) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it

findings.evidence:
The `api_tokens` table holds `user_id`, `token` and `created_at`; the
middleware looks a request's token up with `WHERE token = $1`. Storing the
token as given keeps the lookup a simple indexed equality.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Tokens are stored as given
findings.recommendation: Store only a digest of the token (SHA-256 of the 32 random bytes is enough for high-entropy tokens; no bcrypt needed) in a `token_hash` column with a unique index, hash the presented bearer token in the middleware and look it up with `WHERE token_hash = $1` — still a single indexed equality, so the stated performance reason does not require clear storage. Anyone who reads the `api_tokens` table (a database backup, a replica, a read-only SQL access, an injection elsewhere) otherwise obtains every live bearer credential and can call the API as each user (CWE-312, CWE-256). Show the clear token once at creation, as the spec already requires, and never persist it. Update the design's Alternatives and task 1.1/1.2 accordingly.
findings.title: API tokens are stored in clear in the database

findings.evidence:
To diagnose integration problems, the middleware logs each request's
method, path and headers at `info` level, including `Authorization`, so
support can see which token an integration sent.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Every request is logged with its headers
findings.recommendation: Never log the `Authorization` header (nor `Cookie` / other credential headers): redact it to its scheme (`Bearer [redacted]`) or log a non-reversible identifier of the token (its row id or a short prefix of its hash) so support can still tell which token was sent. As designed, anyone with read access to the info-level logs — support staff, the log pipeline, a log aggregation vendor — collects every user's bearer token and can replay it against the API (CWE-532); with revocation deferred, a token leaked this way stays valid forever. Task 1.3's test `logs_requests` should assert that the token value never appears in the log output.
findings.title: The Authorization header, and so every API token, is written to the logs

findings.recommendation: The proposal's own motivation is that "a leaked integration exposes the account", yet with revocation deferred and no expiry in the design, a token that leaks (through the logs of R-security-2, a compromised integration, or the table of R-security-1) grants permanent API access as the user, and changing the password does not stop it. Either ship a minimal delete of the user's own tokens with this change, or give tokens an expiry (`expires_at` checked by the middleware) until the revocation change lands; the Risks entry "revoking the old one comes with the later revocation change" should state this exposure explicitly if the deferral is kept.
findings.title: A leaked token can never be invalidated: no revocation and no expiry
